claims.text: Adding 0.5 wt% Y to a Co–Cr–Fe–Ni–Al multiprincipal-element alloy enhances its oxidation resistance.
Y addition promotes segregation of Y to grain boundaries in the forming oxide scale.
The protective oxide scale is primarily Al2O3 and/or Cr2O3.
Y segregation stabilizes the oxide scale by improving its adhesion.
Y segregation reduces crack propagation in the oxide scale.
The Y-stabilized scale limits oxygen diffusion and thereby preserves high-temperature material integrity.
The proposed controlled intervention is a 0.5 wt% Y addition while holding processing and specimen geometry constant.
The relevant structural mediator is a continuous, adherent, and slow-growing oxide scale with Y-modified grain boundaries.
High-resolution TEM and EDS mapping can be used to determine whether Y is segregated at oxide-scale grain boundaries.
Y segregation enhances interfacial bonding in the oxide scale.
Y segregation suppresses microcrack initiation and propagation.
Suppression of microcracking improves scale adhesion and reduces spallation during thermal cycling.
Improved adhesion and reduced spallation limit oxygen ingress and internal oxidation.
The Y-doped alloy is predicted to have a lower oxidation growth rate than the baseline alloy.
The Y-doped alloy is predicted to undergo fewer spallation events during cyclic oxidation than the baseline alloy.
The Y-doped alloy is predicted to retain better mechanical integrity at high temperature than the baseline alloy.
The predicted benefits of Y should occur consistently from 800°C to 1100°C in dry oxygen under both isothermal and cyclic exposure.
A joint absence of reduced oxidation growth, improved scale adherence, and enhanced grain-boundary Y segregation would falsify the proposed reactive-element mechanism.

contradictions.description: The Y-bearing alloy is called compositionally identical to the baseline even though adding 0.5 wt% Y necessarily changes its composition. This would be coherent if stated as identical in all non-Y constituents or if Y replaced a specified fraction of another element.
